plan.angle: Keep the plan, with these changes. Ch3: the insulin/sulfonylurea risk in label wording, plus a separately tagged diabetes-guidance source for alcohol's own effect on blood sugar. Ch1: say 'the label doesn't specifically address alcohol' if that's what the label shows. Ch5: alcohol as a pancreatitis risk factor only with an NHS or NIDDK tag. Ch6: only fetched, verified trials, each labelled by drug, population and size. Cut the VA trial unless its registry record is cited. Add a low-blood-sugar emergency line: confusion, fainting or being unable to eat or drink → your local emergency number.

plan.why:
Next topic on the playbook's Lane A list, and holiday-party searches rise from Nov 20. It's evergreen and rests on the label; no alcohol long video exists in the last 30 days. | fact-check: This topic is on the playbook list and has real search demand. Framed this way (no safe amount, no drink counts, prescriber conversation) it is safe under YouTube policy. Four fixes before scripting:
(a) Hypoglycemia. The label's line about higher low-blood-sugar risk is about tirzepatide used with insulin or a sulfonylurea. As far as I know, the label says nothing about alcohol. So 'why alcohol matters there' must come from diabetes guidance (for example a CDC, NHS or Diabetes UK page on alcohol and hypoglycemia), tagged to that source, and never tagged to the label.
(b) Chapter 1. If the Zepbound PI and Medication Guide (rev. 28 Aug 2026) print no alcohol wording, the script must say plainly that the label doesn't specifically address alcohol. It must not suggest that silence means it's fine or that it's risky.
(c) Pancreatitis. Drop alcohol as a risk factor unless a cited NHS or NIDDK pancreatitis page is the tag. Don't tag it to the label.
(d) Chapter 6. Name only trials you can verify: the small semaglutide RCT in adults with alcohol use disorder (Hendershot et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2025, about 48 participants, lab drinking measures) and the exenatide trial (Klausen et al., JCI Insight 2022: no effect on heavy-drinking days overall). Each gets its drug, population and size. Mention the 'VA trial' only if a ClinicalTrials.gov record is fetched and cited. Otherwise cut it. Write 'isn't approved for alcohol use disorder', with no 'yet'.
The thumbnail 'ONE DRINK?' is acceptable as a question, but the script must never answer it with a number.

package.description:
Can you drink alcohol on tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound)? The US label doesn't specifically address alcohol. But three of its warnings matter on a night out: low blood sugar, dehydration and pancreatitis.
If you also use insulin or a sulfonylurea, the label says your risk of low blood sugar may be higher.

Low blood sugar signs plus confusion, fainting, or can't eat or drink? Call your local emergency number.
Severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting? Stop using tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider right away.
Can't keep fluids down? Call your prescriber.

Sources:
Zepbound label, DailyMed (revised 28 Aug 2026): https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=487cd7e7-434c-4925-99fa-aa80b1cc776b
NHS, Low blood sugar (reviewed 03 Aug 2023): https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/low-blood-sugar-hypoglycaemia/
NHS, Dehydration (reviewed 01 May 2026): https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/dehydration/

#tirzepatide

For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop, switch, or change your medicine on your own.
Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

script.working_title: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) and Alcohol: What to Know
script.hook_pattern: Direct question with the answer first (the label doesn't specifically address alcohol), a second concrete payoff at 15–30 s (low blood sugar risk with insulin or a sulfonylurea), a one-sentence open loop (two real trials at the end), then a visceral 'you' scenario (the birthday dinner glass)

scenes.narration: Can you drink alcohol while you're on tirzepatide, whether it's Mounjaro or Zepbound?
scenes.retention_device: Direct question from the title in sentence 1

scenes.narration: Here's the short answer. The US label doesn't specifically address alcohol. It doesn't say a drink is fine, and it doesn't forbid one.

visual.myth: The label has an alcohol rule
visual.fact: The US label doesn't specifically address alcohol

scenes.retention_device: Short answer delivered by about 13 s

scenes.narration: But three warnings in that label matter on a night out: low blood sugar, dehydration, and pancreatitis.
Here's the first one. If you also use insulin or a sulfonylurea, the label says your risk of low blood sugar may be higher.
scenes.on_screen_text: Low blood sugar risk may rise

items: Low blood sugar risk may be higher

scenes.narration: And separately, diabetes guidance lists drinking a lot of alcohol, especially without food, as a cause of low blood sugar. Two risks, stacking.
scenes.on_screen_text: Diabetes guidance: a lot of alcohol can cause lows

visual.stock_query: two blocks stacking, pill and glass

scenes.narration: Stay for the last chapter, where two real trials test whether these medicines change how much people drink.
scenes.on_screen_text: Two real trials, at the end

visual.stock_query: two sealed trial folders, question mark

scenes.retention_device: One-sentence open loop, paid off in chapter 'Can it change drinking?'

scenes.narration: First, picture a friend's birthday dinner. The table's loud, someone's pouring, and a glass lands in front of you.
scenes.on_screen_text: A glass lands in front of you

scenes.narration: And you hesitate. Nobody's judging. You've just had a queasy week, and you're not sure how your body will react.

visual.stock_query: person hesitating at table, gentle worry

scenes.narration: If you've felt that little knot of worry, you're not alone. It's a smart question, and it deserves a real answer.
So let's follow someone through it. Imagine Priya, forty-nine. She uses tirzepatide, she has type two diabetes, and she also takes a sulfonylurea.

visual.stock_query: hypothetical woman at kitchen table, thoughtful

scenes.narration: Priya's question is probably yours too: what actually changes when alcohol meets this medicine?
scenes.retention_device: Question to the viewer before chapter change

scenes.narration: Let's start with the source itself, the US prescribing information. I'm reading the Zepbound label, revised in August twenty twenty-six.
It's long. It covers warnings, side effects, and drug interactions. But there's no part that specifically addresses alcohol.
Here's what that silence means, and what it doesn't. It doesn't mean alcohol is proven safe with tirzepatide. And it doesn't mean it's proven risky.

visual.myth: No alcohol section means it's fine, or that it's dangerous
visual.fact: It means neither. The label doesn't specifically address it.

scenes.narration: It means the decision belongs in a conversation with your prescriber, who knows your other medicines and your health.
Think of it like a weather forecast that never mentions your picnic. It still tells you when rain is coming.

visual.stock_query: weather map with rain, picnic basket

scenes.narration: And this label does warn about three things that alcohol can pile on top of. That's where it gets useful.

visual.stock_query: three signposts on a winding road

scenes.section: Your stomach on a night out
scenes.narration: Start with your stomach, because stomach side effects are among the most common ones in the label.

scenes.section: Your stomach on a night out
scenes.narration: In two placebo-controlled trials in adults with obesity or overweight, nausea affected twenty-five to twenty-nine percent of people across tirzepatide doses. On placebo, it was eight percent.

scenes.section: Your stomach on a night out
scenes.narration: Diarrhea was nineteen to twenty-three percent, versus eight percent on placebo. Vomiting was eight to thirteen percent, versus two percent.

visual.stock_query: two bar charts side by side

scenes.section: Your stomach on a night out
scenes.narration: One of those trials excluded type two diabetes. The other enrolled only people who had it.

visual.stock_query: two trial groups of cartoon adults

scenes.section: Your stomach on a night out
scenes.narration: The label also notes that tirzepatide delays gastric emptying. In plain words, your stomach empties more slowly than it used to.

scenes.section: Your stomach on a night out
scenes.narration: Then add alcohol. The NHS lists alcohol among the food and drink that can bring on heartburn and acid reflux.

visual.stock_query: cocktail glass beside fiery heartburn icon

scenes.section: Your stomach on a night out
scenes.narration: So for Priya, a rich dinner with cocktails in the week after a dose step-up isn't a moral failing. It's just a lot to ask of a stomach that's working differently.

visual.stock_query: woman at dinner, rich food, queasy

scenes.section: Your stomach on a night out
scenes.narration: That's not a reason to panic. It's a reason to notice how your own body responds, and to tell your prescriber if stomach side effects are hard to manage.

scenes.section: Your stomach on a night out
scenes.narration: But your stomach is the part you can feel. The next risk is one you might not notice until it's already happening.
scenes.on_screen_text: The risk you might not feel

scenes.narration: Back to Priya's sulfonylurea. If you have diabetes, this chapter matters most.

visual.stock_query: blood sugar meter beside calm woman

scenes.narration: The label says using tirzepatide with insulin or a sulfonylurea may raise your risk of low blood sugar, including severe low blood sugar.

items: May raise low blood sugar risk, including severe

scenes.narration: If you're not sure whether one of your diabetes medicines is a sulfonylurea, your pharmacist can tell you in seconds.
Here's a detail people miss. That label warning is about tirzepatide plus those medicines. It doesn't mention alcohol.

visual.myth: The label warns about alcohol and low blood sugar
visual.fact: Its warning is about tirzepatide plus insulin or a sulfonylurea

scenes.narration: Alcohol's own effect comes from diabetes guidance. The NHS says people with diabetes can get low blood sugar if they drink a lot of alcohol, particularly without eating.
scenes.on_screen_text: NHS: a lot of alcohol can cause lows

visual.stock_query: blood sugar arrow dipping, glass nearby

scenes.narration: In the US, the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases lists drinking too much alcohol without enough food as a cause of low blood sugar. It adds that alcohol can keep you from feeling the first symptoms.
scenes.on_screen_text: NIDDK: too much alcohol, too little food

visual.stock_query: health institute building, sugar arrow down

scenes.retention_device: Second market source plus a surprising detail

scenes.narration: So for Priya, two things can stack: a medicine combination the label flags, and drinking a lot, which diabetes guidance flags on its own.

visual.stock_query: two flags stacking on a tower

scenes.narration: But here's where it gets weird.
The label's list of low blood sugar signs includes dizziness, slurred speech, confusion, drowsiness, and shakiness.
Read that list again with a drink in your hand. Slurred speech. Confusion. Dizziness. Some of these signs can look a lot like having had too much, so the people around you could misread them.

visual.stock_query: party friends misreading a dizzy guest

scenes.narration: So this combination deserves a plan. The risk isn't only the drink. It's that low blood sugar could be misread as the drink.
So if Priya drinks, someone with her should know she has diabetes and what low blood sugar looks like. That's a calm, practical step.
And here's an emergency line. If someone with low blood sugar signs is confused, faints, or can't eat or drink, call your local emergency number.
scenes.on_screen_text: Low blood sugar signs plus confusion, fainting, or can't eat or drink? Call your local emergency number.

scenes.narration: Before drinking at all, Priya can ask her prescriber what her plan should be, with her specific diabetes medicines in mind.
Low blood sugar is the big risk for people on those other medicines. The next one can affect anyone on tirzepatide.
Let's talk about water, because this is where alcohol and stomach side effects quietly team up.
The label warns that nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea can lead to dehydration. And if dehydration is severe, it could cause acute kidney injury.
The patient guide in that label says it's important to drink fluids to help reduce your chance of dehydration.

visual.stock_query: glass of water beside patient leaflet

scenes.narration: Next, look at the NHS list of things that can cause dehydration. It includes being sick or having diarrhoea. It also includes drinking too much alcohol.
Notice the overlap. On a day you've been sick or had diarrhea, alcohol is one more item from that same list.

visual.stock_query: two overlapping circles, water drop center

scenes.narration: Picture a bathtub with the plug half out. Vomiting or diarrhea pulls the plug a little further. Alcohol is another drain, not a refill.

visual.stock_query: cartoon bathtub draining, plug half out

scenes.narration: Early signs the NHS lists include feeling thirsty, dark yellow, strong-smelling pee, peeing less often, feeling dizzy or tired, and a dry mouth.

The NHS says to get urgent medical help if you feel unusually tired, you're dizzy when you stand up and it doesn't go away, or you're peeing less than normal. And if someone is confused or unusually sleepy, call your local emergency number.
scenes.on_screen_text: Unusually tired, dizziness on standing that doesn't go away, or peeing less than normal? Get urgent help. Confused or unusually sleepy? Call your local emergency number.

visual.stock_query: concerned person at urgent care door

scenes.narration: And if you've been vomiting or had diarrhea and can't keep fluids down, call your prescriber. Fluid loss from vomiting or diarrhea is what the label's dehydration and kidney warning is about.
scenes.on_screen_text: Can't keep fluids down? Call your prescriber

scenes.narration: Which brings us to the warning sign that matters most, and a place where alcohol has its own history.
Pancreatitis means inflammation of the pancreas. The tirzepatide label includes a warning about acute pancreatitis.
Separately, the NHS says the most common causes of acute pancreatitis are gallstones and drinking a lot of alcohol.
To be clear, that's a general fact about pancreatitis. It isn't a finding about tirzepatide and alcohol together.
scenes.on_screen_text: General fact, not a combo finding

visual.myth: Studies show tirzepatide plus alcohol causes pancreatitis
visual.fact: Alcohol is a general pancreatitis cause, not a tested combination finding

scenes.narration: Here's the sign to know, from the label. Severe pain in your stomach area that won't go away, with or without vomiting. You may feel it spread to your back.
scenes.on_screen_text: Severe pain that won't go away

visual.stock_query: person holding tummy, arrow to back

scenes.narration: If that happens, stop using tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider right away.
scenes.on_screen_text: Severe stomach pain that won't go away? Stop using tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider right away.

scenes.narration: Severe pain that won't go away is never something to sleep off after a night out. It's a phone call.

visual.stock_query: person reaching for phone at night

scenes.narration: That's the safety side, all from the label and established guidance. But you came with a second question, and I promised you two real trials.
scenes.retention_device: Return to the main open loop

scenes.narration: Maybe you've seen headlines saying GLP-1 medicines make people lose interest in alcohol. Maybe you've wondered if it's happening to you.
Researchers got curious because animal studies suggested GLP-1 medicines might reduce alcohol intake. But animals aren't people, so human trials matter.
First, exenatide, an older GLP-1 medicine. A Danish trial gave it or a placebo to one hundred twenty-seven adults with alcohol use disorder for twenty-six weeks.

visual.stat_label: Adults with alcohol use disorder, 26 weeks

scenes.narration: Both groups also got talk therapy. The main result: no difference in heavy drinking days overall, compared with placebo.

visual.stat_label: Heavy drinking days, exenatide vs placebo
visual.stock_query: two level bars side by side

scenes.narration: An exploratory look hinted at an effect in participants with obesity. But exploratory means it raises a question. It doesn't answer one.
scenes.on_screen_text: Exploratory: a question, not an answer

scenes.narration: Then the second trial, the one that made headlines.

In a trial published in JAMA Psychiatry in twenty twenty-five, forty-eight adults with alcohol use disorder, who weren't seeking treatment, were randomized to low-dose semaglutide or placebo for nine weeks.

visual.stat_label: Adults with alcohol use disorder, 9 weeks

scenes.narration: At the end, in a lab drinking session, people on semaglutide drank less alcohol than people on placebo.
scenes.on_screen_text: Semaglutide group drank less in lab

visual.stock_query: cartoon researchers in tidy lab session

scenes.narration: That's a genuinely interesting signal. But it's forty-eight people, nine weeks, and a lab setting. Not daily life over years.
And notice what's missing. Neither trial tested tirzepatide. Tirzepatide isn't approved for alcohol use disorder.

visual.fact: Tirzepatide isn't approved for alcohol use disorder

scenes.narration: So the honest answer to the big question: the early trials are small, mixed, and intriguing. They're a reason for bigger studies, not proof.

visual.stock_query: scale with small trials, big question

scenes.narration: If Priya notices she wants wine less, that's worth mentioning to her doctor. It's not a reason to treat tirzepatide as an alcohol treatment.
And if drinking itself worries you, that's a real health conversation, and you deserve support. Talk to your doctor, or your local alcohol support service.
Let's bring it home for Priya, and for you. Five things to take with you.
One. Ask your prescriber about alcohol before you drink, especially if you use insulin or a sulfonylurea.

visual.stat_label: Ask your prescriber before you drink

scenes.narration: Two. Know the low blood sugar signs, and make sure someone with you knows them too.

visual.stat_label: Know low blood sugar signs; tell someone

scenes.narration: Three. On days with vomiting or diarrhea, focus on fluids. Alcohol is on the dehydration list for a reason.

visual.stat_label: Fluids first on vomiting or diarrhea days

scenes.narration: Four. Notice what alcohol does to your stomach on this medicine, and tell your prescriber if side effects are hard to manage.

visual.stat_label: Notice your stomach; tell your prescriber

scenes.narration: Five. Severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting, means stop using tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider right away.
scenes.on_screen_text: Severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting? Stop using tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider right away.

visual.stat_label: Severe stomach pain: stop, call right away

scenes.narration: Remember Priya at that birthday dinner? She doesn't need fear. She needs a plan, and she has one. So do you.
For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop, switch, or change your medicine on your own.
scenes.on_screen_text: For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop, switch, or change your medicine on your own.

visual.stock_query: calm Medi with gentle stop hand

scenes.narration: Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
scenes.on_screen_text: Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary:
I checked every factual claim I could against the source behind it, and they hold up. The script passes. Two wording fixes are optional.

**What the sources confirm**
- **No alcohol in the label:** the Zepbound US label (revised 8/2026, per DailyMed) never mentions alcohol, so s02, s13, s14 and s30 are accurate.
- **Stomach side-effect rates (s19–s20):** these match the label table for Studies 1 and 2. Nausea was 25/29/28% vs 8% on placebo, diarrhea 19/21/23% vs 8%, and vomiting 8/11/13% vs 2%.
- **Other label wording:**
  - The label says tirzepatide delays gastric emptying.
  - The low blood sugar warning is about tirzepatide used with insulin or a sulfonylurea.
  - The low blood sugar signs, the dehydration/kidney warning and the "drink fluids" line match the label and Medication Guide.
  - The pancreatitis sign is quoted correctly, including "with or without vomiting", spreading to the back, and "stop and call right away".
- **NHS low blood sugar page (s31):** it says "drink a lot of alcohol, particularly without eating".
- **NIDDK page (s32):** it says "Drinking too much alcohol without enough food" and that alcohol "can keep you from feeling the first symptoms".
- **NHS dehydration page (s45, s48, s49):** the causes list ("been sick or have diarrhoea", "drunk too much alcohol"), the symptoms, and both the urgent-help and 999 lists match.
- **NHS acute pancreatitis page (s53):** gallstones and "drinking a lot of alcohol" are the most common causes.
- **NHS heartburn page (s23):** alcohol is listed as a trigger.
- **The two trials:**
  - Hendershot, JAMA Psychiatry 2025 (PMID 39937469): 48 adults with alcohol use disorder who weren't seeking treatment, on low-dose semaglutide or placebo for 9 weeks. Alcohol drunk in the lab session went down.
  - Klausen, JCI Insight 2022 (PMID 36066977): 127 adults seeking treatment, all also getting talk therapy (CBT), for 26 weeks. There was no difference in heavy drinking days overall, but an effect showed up in people with a BMI over 30. The script calls that an exploratory finding, which is appropriately cautious.

**Framing and safety**
- The script keeps the label's warnings and the general alcohol guidance clearly apart (s30, s33, s54).
- It is clear that neither trial tested tirzepatide and that tirzepatide isn't approved for alcohol use disorder.
- It never gives a "safe amount" of alcohol.
- It includes the low blood sugar caveat for people on insulin or a sulfonylurea, emergency lines with the trigger named and "right away", the don't-stop line scoped to non-emergencies, the disclaimer and prescriber line in the right order, and an alcohol-support line.
- Priya is clearly hypothetical and isn't shamed.

**Source access:** the two PubMed links only showed a cookie page to my tool, so I confirmed both records through Europe PMC. Both IDs are correct.

issues.claim: Some of these signs overlap with having had too much, so the people around you could misread them.
issues.problem: This is a reasonable inference, but no source in the list says it. It stays acceptable because it isn't tagged to a source and it's worded cautiously ("could").
issues.fix: Keep it as is with no source tag. If you want it tighter: "Some of these signs can look a lot like having had too much, so the people around you could misread them."

issues.claim: That's the situation the kidney warning is about.
issues.problem: This slightly narrows the label. Its warning is about fluid loss from nausea, vomiting or diarrhea leading to dehydration, and through that to kidney injury. "Can't keep fluids down" is our own way of putting it.
issues.fix: Replace the second sentence with: "Fluid loss from vomiting or diarrhea is what the label's dehydration and kidney warning is about."

audio.soundNotes: Music is already sitting right in the -12/-15dB target window (measured -13.5 under voice and in pauses), so kept the multiplier at 1.0 rather than risk pushing it louder. The main fix was a cluster of SFX cues that measured far too hot against the voice (several between -3.7 and -9.8 dB, i.e. nearly as loud as the narrator) scattered through the kidney/pancreatitis and trial-data sections — pulled those down toward the -16dB felt zone. Also thinned the densest "chip reveal" bursts (90s, 152s, 268s, 344s, 421s, 601s) where 5–8 pops/blips were landing within ~1–2 seconds; dropped the most redundant ones so no moment has more than 3–4 effects. Left the already-good practice of ducking SFX way down under the pancreatitis/low-blood-sugar warning lines (several cues already sit at -14 to -63dB there) untouched since that matches the "thin out on serious moments" rule. Added five bespoke accents for the story beats the stock kit can't cover: a toast-like clink on the opening hook, a slow heartbeat under "Confused or very sleepy?", a low unease drone under the pancreatitis warning, an archival paper-rustle for the trials section, and a bright chime on the closing watch-next card.

thumbnail.reasoning:
All three candidates are legible at phone size (short, bold 2-4 word headlines, no cutoffs), none give away the answer, none literally repeat the title's words, and faces/design match the emotional tone of their text. 

Row #0 "ONE GLASS. THEN?" directly mirrors the title's exact question ("Can you drink?") with a broad, universally relatable felt-moment hook (the worried face after one drink), keeping the curiosity gap wide open without narrowing the audience. The reaction-face layout and purple glow give strong contrast and a single clear focal point.

Row #1 "ON INSULIN TOO?" is accurate to the label's low-blood-sugar caveat and uses good loss-aversion framing with a caution-tape visual, but it narrows the implied audience to insulin/sulfonylurea users, which is a subset of viewers interested in the broader alcohol question the title promises — slightly weaker broad-appeal CTR, though still legible and non-misleading.

Row #2 "WHAT CHANGES?" is a pure mystery play with a bottle silhouette and giant question mark; it's clean and legible but lacks a face or felt tension, making it the least emotionally gripping of the three, and "mystery" silhouette layouts have less proven pull than state-change or reaction formats in our own data.

Best pick: Row #0, for the strongest combination of broad relevance, emotional pull, and faithful match to the title's question, while keeping the curiosity gap open.

issues.problem: This keeps the curiosity gap honestly and matches the 'a glass lands in front of you' scene. But the video never says what one glass does. The alcohol-related lows it covers come from drinking 'a lot' or 'too much' alcohol. A viewer could read the thumbnail as promising a one-drink verdict, or as hinting that a single glass is dangerous. That's slight over-promising, not a false claim.
issues.fix: Optional: replace with "A DRINK ON THIS?" (with the face showing hesitation and a glass as the one big object). Or keep "ONE GLASS. THEN?" as it is. It's acceptable.
